notes: Class 9 geography, generated by tooling/scripts/build_fresh_papers.py. Marks are printed against each question and total 22 over the markable entries, against a stated maximum of 30 -- the paper is internally inconsistent, which is deliberate and realistic. Question 2 is a stem with a river sketch drawn between it and its roman sub-parts. Two entries carry no mark truth and both say why: the stem asks nothing, and 2 (i) cannot be marked by anybody because the figure does not depict a nameable landform at position A. Question 3 asks for a labelled sketch and the student leaves it blank, which is the case worth watching -- the correct mark is zero, and the system will also return zero, but for the unrelated reason that it refuses to grade drawings from text. A right number reached by a wrong route is still a fault, and it is invisible in any mark-error figure.

questions.key: Relief (orographic), convectional and frontal, with where each occurs: relief on windward slopes near coasts, convectional in hot regions in the afternoon, frontal where warm and cold air masses meet. One mark per named type with its location.
questions.note: All three named and all three located. Nothing to withhold, so no band.

questions.excluded_reason: A stem. It introduces (i) and (ii), carries no marks of its own and asks nothing, so there is no mark to be right or wrong about. Included in truth so that a run reporting it as unanswered is visible as a fault.

Indeterminate, not unmarked. The figure is two bezier curves with the letters A, B and N placed on it; A sits at the narrow upstream end and depicts no specific landform, so no answer to 'name the landform at A' can be scored right or wrong without me inventing what the sketch was supposed to show. Scoring it would put my guess into the denominator of every figure downstream. Fix the fixture, not the truth: give the generator a figure with an identifiable feature at A.

questions.key: Formation of the feature at B. B sits where the sketched channel widens at its downstream end, so a delta is the reading the figure supports: reduced velocity on meeting standing water, deposition of the sediment load, progressive build-up of new low-lying land at the mouth.
questions.note: Gives velocity loss, deposition, accumulation into new land, and names the delta. Self-contained and correct as an account of delta formation regardless of how the figure is read, which is why this one is scored where 2 (i) is not.

questions.key: A labelled sketch of a meander: fastest flow on the outside of the bend, erosion and a river cliff there, slack water and deposition forming a slip-off slope on the inside. Marks are for the drawing and its labels.
questions.note: Left entirely blank. Truth is zero because nothing was drawn, NOT because the question is a drawing. Any run that reports zero here should be checked for which of the two reasons it gave -- see the document note.

questions.key: Two reasons, developed, for continued floodplain settlement: fertile alluvial soil for farming, flat land cheap to build on, water supply, transport and trade routes.
questions.note: Three reasons given where two were asked for, each with its consequence attached. Band allows a marker who wants explicit acknowledgement of the risk being traded off to hold one back.

questions.key: Both sides of the distinction plus one example each. Weathering: in-situ breakdown with no transport -- freeze-thaw. Erosion: removal and transport of the loosened material -- a river undercutting its bank.
questions.note: Both definitions correct, the in-situ versus transported contrast made explicitly, and a valid example on each side. This is the contrast case answered in full, so nothing to withhold.
